cells.tense: You're deciding what to keep and what to let go, and it's working here.
cells.ask: Hand off one thing you've been holding, just the handing, and watch whether the ground still feels like yours afterward.
cells.core:
You keep what's worth keeping and you release the rest, and letting a thing go doesn't feel like losing it. That's how anything starts growing again. You've got a sense of which is which that doesn't argue with you — you pick up a thing, hold it a second, and know.

That's rare, and it's the whole reason what you have keeps being worth having. You're also pointed at something you actually want, and you're not pretending otherwise. That pull tells you what to hold and what to put down. Nothing needs fixing here. Keep one thing you'd otherwise shed this week, just to stay familiar with choosing.
cells.sheetLine: You know what to keep and what to let go, and it works.
cells.verb: Releasing what's finished so what's still good can keep growing
cells.place: Standing in the pull of what you're drawn toward, steering by what you actually want

cells.tense: You're forcing the change before it's ready, bracing at a future you can't write in.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that's still alive and leave it alone for a day, then tell someone what you felt while it sat there.
cells.core:
You're clearing before the season turns. Somewhere up ahead you can see the ending already done, the new growth already up, and you're working backwards from it — pulling things out before they've finished, forcing the next thing before it's ready. Every push is meant to get there faster, and it's the speed that's hurting you.

Endings that go early don't come back right. What grows has to grow on its own clock, and you can feel that in everything except your own timing. You can feel other people's timing fine — when a friend needs a night, when the room needs quiet. That skill is right there. Aim it at the things you're holding.

cells.tense: A door closed behind you and you're still standing at it.
cells.ask: Take one small, ordinary task from start to finish today, then let yourself feel the finished thing before you look for what's next.
cells.core:
You stopped rearranging things a while back — stopped clearing, stopped deciding what stays. Somewhere along the way you put it down, and you've been standing on the same spot ever since. Nothing new has started because nothing old has been let go of.

The pull toward what you want didn't go out. You just quit following it, and it's weaker than it used to be. So don't start with the clearing. Start with one small thing you can carry to the end today and actually finish. That movement is what turns the light back on, and then you'll be able to see what's finished and what isn't.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped sorting what stays, and everything sits where it landed.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room you're already writing in.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've decided to let go of this year and say out loud that it was your call.
cells.core:
You're already deciding what stays and what goes here, in how you live and how you hand things on. But your own story says it's just how things turned out. Offerings you made, endings you called.

That's the part you haven't claimed. Not the doing — the deciding. You keep describing your choices like they were nobody's, and around you it all runs smoothly, which is why nobody corrects you, including you. The one missing piece is the sentence "that was mine." Once you say it, what you've been aiming at gets easier to see, and your next move comes from a place you can name.
cells.sheetLine: The call was yours. Your account of it leaves you out.

A reader could reasonably say nothing good was ever kept, so nothing was worth passing on; the asks still work then, since offering one thing and letting what's held stay held cost nothing to try.
